new_statements.relation_note: Catalog initial stress (fixed initial) matches Terrill's default ('Most words have stress on their initial syllable'; WALS 14A/15A/17A code Lavukaleve Initial / Fixed, no weight / Trochaic). Terrill adds that assignment is only partly fixed: a small lexical residue of second- and third-syllable words, loans keeping source stress, alternating secondary stress, and Possessive-prefix stress shifts. Caveats: (1) the copy opened is the open-access 1999 ANU PhD thesis that became the 2003 Mouton book, not the Mouton edition itself (De Gruyter page returned an AWS WAF bot challenge on two attempts; the thesis PDF is 97.4 MB, over the 80 MB cap, so the repository's extracted-text bitstream was read…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the initial syllable of the word by default (almost all CVCV words, all CVCV nouns); a small lexically specified set has second-syllable stress (old CV-reduplications like tu'tuk, va'var, le'lenga invariably; many CVCVC disyllables like ni'kol, fa'luk, fo'sal; recent loans keep source-language stress) and a very few words have third-syllable stress (fela'koe, mala'gula, lau'rario, mita'keu). No weight sensitivity is invoked. In complex words the root keeps its stress and affixes are unstressed, except that Possessive prefixes take the stress on monosyllabic nouns ('o-ta 'its time') and in Possessor-subject verb forms ('ngavoe 'I came').
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 29: 'Secondary stress occurs every second syllable in either direction from the syllable with primary stress' (examples 'mano,giri,giri 'seagull sp.', lovi,tan 'eel sp.', mita'keu 'dog'), i.e. alternating secondary stress radiating from the primary.
new_statements.exceptions: Second-syllable stress in old reduplications CVαCVβ.. (invariably), many CVCVC disyllables (but not all: 'legis, 'mikat, 'hamus), a few third-syllable words; recent borrowings keep the source-language stress even after epenthesis ('kavis, ta'rak); stress shifts to a Possessive prefix on monosyllabic nouns and on verbs in the Possessor-subject construction (occasionally spreading to ordinary subject prefixes, 'ovo); shouted utterances replace the final vowel by /ou/ and shift stress to the penult (§2.9); verb compounds and serial verbs carry one stress per verb. Terrill notes stress vs identical-vowel sequences is sometimes hard to hear (2.7.3).
new_statements.identity_note: Terrill states (thesis p. 10-11) that her corpus 'consists entirely of the speech variety of the West Russells' (Mane village and other West Russells villages); no data from the Eastern villages (Loun, Alokan). The work opened is the 1999 ANU PhD thesis version of the 2003 Mouton grammar; page locators are thesis pages.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on placement: Terrill (1999/2003) and the catalog (and WALS 14A/15A/16A/17A: Initial, fixed, no weight, trochaic) all put default primary stress on the initial syllable. The only tension is in framing: Terrill's overview calls stress 'unpredictable, although it most commonly falls on the initial syllable' (p. 11) and the phonology chapter calls assignment 'partly fixed and partly lexically assigned' (p. 27), i.e. initial stress is a strong default with a lexically listed residue (second-syllable in old reduplications, some CVCVC disyllables and loans; a few third-syllable words), whereas the catalog records a plain fixed: initial syllable rule with no exceptions. The second-syllable class is small (Terrill: 'something around 0.05% in the corpus', as scanned), so fixed: initial syllable remains the best single reading.
